title: Tsakonian: the one living descendant of a Doric dialect
lead: In a handful of mountain villages above the Argolic Gulf, on the eastern slopes of Mount Parnon, older people still speak **Τσακώνικα**. It is the only form of Greek alive today that does not come mainly from the Hellenistic Koine: it continues, with heavy Koine influence, the ancient **Laconian Doric** of Sparta. To a speaker of Standard Greek it is largely unintelligible, which is why many linguists treat it as a separate Hellenic language.
facts: **Τσακωνιά**, in Kynouria (Arcadia). South: **Λεωνίδιο**, Πραματευτή, Μέλανα, Σαπουνακέικα, Τυρός, Πραστός, Βασκίνα. North: **Καστάνιτσα**, Σίταινα. A third variety was spoken until about 1970 in two villages on the Sea of Marmara (Propontis), whose people moved to Greece in 1924.
A few hundred fluent, mostly elderly speakers (estimates of 200–1,000 by 2007) and more semi-speakers; Southern Tsakonian is the best preserved.
Laconian Doric, mixed with Koine; the core vocabulary remains recognisably Doric.
No official status; some teaching materials, bilingual signs in Leonidio, liturgy and the Lord's Prayer translated.

sections.text: Ancient Laconian was one of the Doric dialects that resisted the Koine longest. Byzantine sources speak of the **Τσάκωνες** as a distinct people of the south-eastern Peloponnese, and Tsakonian was once spoken over a wider area, including the Laconian coast; the 17th-century Ottoman traveller Evliya Çelebi recorded forms that may belong to a lost western variety. Mountain isolation kept the language intact for centuries. During the War of Independence the centre of Tsakonia moved from Prastos to coastal Leonidio, and from the 19th century schooling, roads, and from the 1950s electricity, radio and television, brought Standard Greek into every house. Fluent speakers fell from many thousands to a few hundred within a century.

sections.h: Verbs: 'I am bringing' with a participle
sections.text: Tsakonian forms its present and imperfect not with endings but with the verb 'to be' plus a **participle** that agrees with the subject in gender, much like English *I am bringing*. A man says **ένει φερήκχου**, a woman **ένει φερήκχα** 'I bring'. In the old texts the copula is also written **έμι** (ancient εἰμί). The aorist, by contrast, is the one tense formed with endings as in ancient Greek.
sections.after: Past of 'to be': **έμα, έσα, έκη, έμαϊ, έτθαϊ, ήγκιαϊ**. The aorist **ενέγκα** continues ancient **ἤνεγκα** 'I brought', the same root as Pontic **έγκα**. Propontis Tsakonian put the copula after the participle and kept ancient perfect participles in -κώς.

culture.text: Leonidio, the largest Tsakonian town, holds its **Πάσχα** with hundreds of paper lanterns released over the town, and its sweet aubergine, the **μελιτζάνα Τσακώνικη**, has protected designation of origin. Local associations publish Tsakonian dictionaries and grammars (above all Thanasis Kostakis's), run summer classes, and there is a small Tsakonian Wikipedia in development. A street sign in Leonidio tells visitors, in Tsakonian and Greek: 'Our language is Tsakonian. Ask and they'll tell you.'

questions.q: Tsakonian is unique because it descends mainly from…
questions.why: All other living dialects (except perhaps Italiot) come from the Koine.

questions.q: **α μάτη** 'the mother' keeps which Doric feature?
options: Long α where Attic has η
questions.answer: Long α where Attic has η
questions.why: Doric μάτηρ vs Attic μήτηρ; the article α is also Doric (Attic ἡ).

questions.q: How does a woman say 'I bring' in Tsakonian?
questions.why: The present is 'be' + participle, and the participle agrees with the speaker's gender.
